Series::mish¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::mish() const
Series& Series::mish_() const

A Smooth, Non-Monotonic Activation¶

mish() applies

$$ \operatorname{mish}(x)=x\tanh(\log(1+e^x)) $$

elementwise. It keeps large positive values close to the identity, softly suppresses negative values, and permits a small negative output instead of clamping the entire negative half-line to zero. The shallow negative trough is why the function is non-monotonic.

Choose it when a smooth activation with nonzero negative output is useful. Choose hardswish() when a cheaper piecewise-polynomial gate is more important, or selu() when the fixed self-normalizing scale and negative saturation are specifically required.

Type, Shape, And Derivative Contract¶

  • The operation is elementwise and preserves rank, shape, and platform.

  • Floating-point dtype is preserved. Integer and Boolean receivers are promoted to float32, because fractional activation values cannot be represented in their original dtype.

  • Complex input is rejected; the ordered real activation has no unambiguous complex extension in this API.

  • The receiver is not mutated. The returned Series owns a new result.

  • Reverse mode uses the analytic derivative

    $$ \tanh(s)+x,\operatorname{sigmoid}(x)(1-\tanh^2(s)), \qquad s=\operatorname{softplus}(x). $$

    The derivative remains connected for higher-order differentiation.

At very negative input, the result approaches zero from below. At very positive input, it approaches x. The implementation uses the stable softplus() path rather than directly evaluating an overflowing exp(x).

In-Place Form¶

mish_() is the in-place sibling of mish(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — mish_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, 0.0, 2.0});
x.mish_();
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.25250148, 0, 1.943959]

Examples¶

1. Observe both tails and the negative trough¶

const auto x = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.mish());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.1456, -0.3034, 0.0000, 0.8651, 2.9865]

The value at -1 is more negative than at -3, demonstrating the non-monotonic negative region. Positive values increasingly approach the identity.

2. Higher-rank input keeps its structure¶

const auto x = pluss::make_series({{-2.0, 0.0}, {1.0, 3.0}});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.mish());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ -0.2525 0.0000 ⎤
⎣  0.8651 2.9865 ⎦

No axis has special meaning. Every lane is transformed independently.

3. Integer input is promoted¶

const auto y = pluss::make_series({-2, 0, 2}).mish();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, y);

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.2525, 0.0000, 1.9440]

Promotion happens before evaluation, so the negative and positive fractional results are not truncated back to integers.

4. Reverse mode follows the smooth derivative¶

auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 1.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.mish().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0592, 0.6000, 1.0490]

The derivative at zero is exactly 0.6. Near 1, the derivative can exceed one; the activation is not a clipped gate.

5. Complex input fails explicitly¶

try {
  using Complex = std::complex<double>;
  (void)pluss::make_series(
      std::vector<Complex>{{1.0, 1.0}}, {1}).mish();
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::cout << error.what() << '\n';
}

Output¶

mish: complex input is not supported

Performance¶

mish() is linear in numel() and uses exponential, logarithmic, and hyperbolic operations, so it is materially more expensive than piecewise linear activations. The named reverse node avoids retaining every temporary from the forward formula, while recomputing the derivative ingredients only when reverse propagation is requested.

See Also¶

  • softplus() is the smooth positive transform inside Mish.

  • hardswish() is a cheaper piecewise activation.

  • selu() supplies fixed self-normalizing constants.
